newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Coconut Oil - Tight supply seen pushing prices up.
newsitem.headline: Coconut Oil - Tight supply seen pushing prices up.

text.p: Typhoon-battered Philippine coconut oil production is unlikely to recover in the fourth quarter and this will probably push prices higher this week, vegetable oil traders said on Monday.
"I expect prices for forward months to rise further as the prospects of a recovery for Philippine coconut output remain dim," said one Manila-based trader.
Coconut output for the rest of 1996 through until the first quarter of 1997 is likely to remain at current tight levels, the traders said.
Production has been hit hard by a string of typhoons in 1995 which ravaged 300,000 coconut trees on the main island of Luzon.
"Coconut production from the Philippines remain tight. We may only see a recovery in the second quarter of 1997," one trader said.
"With this scenario, I expect coconut oil prices to pick up another $15 for forward months this week," he added.
The private trade group United Coconut Associations of the Philippines (UCAP) said coconut oil prices were traded last week at an average price of US$768.75 per tonne CIF.
Manila traders also forecast that coconut oil prices for nearby months would continue their rise despite the arrival of three vessels carrying an estimated 88,000 tonnes of oil in Europe this week.
The trader said the three vessels were carrying coconut oil from the Philippines and Indonesia.
"The cargoes are for both the U.S. and European markets, which have a demand of 45,000 tonnes each monthly," he said.
One trader said MV Batumi, which is carrying 15,000 tonnes of coconut oil is arriving in Rotterdam today.
Star Sapphire, with a cargo of 35,000 tonnes of coconut oil is scheduled to arrive on Wednesday and Kenwood Park, with a cargo of 38,000 tonnes is arriving on Friday, the trader said.
"Even with the fresh supply of coconut oil in the export market, I don't expect prices to soften as buyers are very hungry for more stocks," the trader said.

"This week will be telling. If demand for the commodity continues despite fresh supplies, then expect prices to continue their rise," he said, adding prices have not reached their peak. "There's still an upside for nearby months."
Traders said they expect the next shipment of coconut oil in Rotterdam on December 21.
"Stolt Sapphire left the country on November 6," the trader said. The volume of oil in the ship was not immediately available.

One trader worried by the sharp rise in coconut oil cautioned: "With few bottoms (ships) going to the export market, coconut oil may become too expensive for its own good. Buyers will soon find out that other vegetable oils are a better deal." "Because of the limited freight space, the local market may experience a glut, and a corresponding price reduction. Tight
supply (of the commodity) in the foreign market, however, will benefit the few exporters," the trader added.
